titleStmt.title: Replication-Driven Resource Sharing in Real-Time Multicore Systems

analytic.title: Replication-Driven Resource Sharing in Real-Time Multicore Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Resource sharing in multicore architectures remains a significant challenge that limits the performance potential of such systems, especially in industrial domains requiring high performance and strict timing guarantees. In this paper, we introduce a novel synchronization protocol called Multi-replicas Time-bounded Consistency (MTC), designed to mitigate the adverse effects of resource sharing among tasks distributed across different cores. MTC achieves this by replicating shared resources while maintaining a bounded level of consistency among replicas within a defined time constraint. We present a response-time analysis of the proposed protocol and demonstrate that MTC can substantially simplify the evaluation of response-time analysis compared to traditional lock-based synchronization methods, offering a potentially more efficient and scalable alternative.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the era of smart automation, the need for computational power has increased significantly due to the extensive use of data to optimize decision making, processes, quality, and machine and robot control. Cloud computing may not be sufficient due to strict industrial requirements, including safety, security, energy consumption, and low latency. Edge computing has been proposed as a solution to provide on-premises computational power for systems with strict industrial requirements. Edge computing can be used to execute resourceintensive applications with different criticality requirements. Some applications might be used to train AI models and run trained models, while others may be used to control machines and robots. For such systems, edge computing requires powerful hardware and efficient use of computing resources to meet the increasing workload and performance demands. Due to the sharing of data, software services, and hardware resources among many software applications executed on computers (e.g., Edge), the advantages provided by powerful computers might be significantly reduced and, in the worst case, might violate the requirements for meeting deadlines for real-time applications. This paper focuses mainly on data sharing, referred to as shared resources, among different realtime software applications/tasks.
Researchers have proposed many solutions for managing and synchronizing tasks' access to shared resources. Lockbased solutions are the most popular alternative, providing

Lock-based approaches cause blocking times for other tasks that require access to resources when those resources are locked. In multiprocessor/multicore architectures, lock-based solutions might hamper the parallel execution of tasks that require access to the same resource, even though parallelism is a key feature of state-of-the-art hardware for boosting performance. When a task locks a shared resource, no other tasks, even those running on other cores, are allowed to access the locked resource, causing tasks to either busy-wait or suspend their execution until the resource is released. Many studies propose different solutions to reduce the impact of blocking times on the timing requirements of real-time tasks [1]- [4]. However, the blocking times imposed by lock-based solutions in multicore systems can significantly affect the timing guarantees required by real-time tasks. In addition, lock-based solutions significantly increase the complexity of timing analysis, requiring very pessimistic assumptions to provide a safe bound for response times. However, the main advantage of using lock-based mechanisms is that they guarantee a high level of data consistency, meaning that at any time, the data stored in a shared resource is the same for all tasks. In addition, lock-based solutions do not require extra memory allocation compared to solutions based on multiple copies or replicas of shared resources.

The wait-free approach [5] is another solution that can eliminate blocking times on tasks due to resource sharing. In this approach, tasks do not interfere with each other when they access shared resources simultaneously. As a result, tasks complete operations on shared resources (read/write) in a bounded number of steps. This can be achieved by using multiple buffers to avoid data corruption. Whenever a write operation is requested, data is saved in an available buffer, while read operations are performed on the most recently updated buffer.

The number of buffers required for each shared resource is proportional to the number of tasks accessing it 1 . As a consequence, tasks that access shared resources may require more memory than the system can provide. However, data consistency cannot be guaranteed using this approach.

The third approach is the lock-free approach [7], [8]. In this method, multiple tasks are allowed to access shared data concurrently without blocking each other, and tasks continue executing until they need to write results or take action. To ensure data consistency, a task checks whether the shared data has changed. If it has, the task re-accesses the data and repeats the process until it successfully writes the data. The main drawback of this approach in real-time systems is the difficulty in bounding the number of retries a task may require to complete its execution over shared resources. Furthermore, the overhead of implementing this approach is higher than that of the other methods.

Regarding data consistency requirements, not all tasks need access to the most recent data; in many cases, older data may still be useful. The impact of using outdated data might be negligible on the quality of service provided by real-time tasks, allowing for relaxed consistency models that reduce system stress. Examples of such applications include control systems, where older data may have a minimal effect on control quality, provided the data age remains within acceptable limits.

In this paper, we propose the MTC protocol, a novel solution that combines lock-based and wait-free approaches to reduce blocking time and memory requirements in multicore systems. The basic idea is to provide fewer replicas per shared resource compared to the wait-free approach. This means that a group of tasks shares a replica of the shared resource, rather than all tasks sharing a single resource (as in the lock-based approach), or each task being assigned its own replica (as in the wait-free approach). As a result, within each group of tasks sharing a replica, tasks may still experience blocking, but the blocking times are shorter than in the lock-based case where only one resource is used.

In addition, data stored in replicas is synchronized periodically to maintain an acceptable level of data consistency. At any given time, the data may not be identical across all replicas of the shared resource; however, periodic synchronization ensures that the data age remains bounded.

A typical application area for MTC is the control systems domain, such as those found in automation and automotive systems. A task implementing a control algorithm may read data from a replica that has not yet been synchronized (i.e., stale data), resulting in what is known as input time delay in control systemsor input jitter if the delay is not constant.

Many methods have been proposed to handle time delays in control systems. Some approaches incorporate the impact of time delays into the control system model used for controller design. The Pade approximation-based method [9] is one such example, used to model time delay effects in the control loop. This model is general, making it suitable for various controller designs, including the well-known PID controller.

Another approach to handling time delays is to dynamically adjust the controller parameters to compensate for timevarying delays. The works presented in [10] and [11] are two examples of mitigating the impact of delays on control systems by adapting controller parameters at runtime.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Many synchronization protocols have been proposed for managing resource sharing in real-time systems. The most well-known lock-based protocols for single processors are the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [12] and the Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [13]. In the domain of multiprocessor systems, Rajkumar presented the Multiprocessor PCP (MPCP) [14], which extends PCP [12] to multiprocessors to synchronize tasks sharing mutually exclusive resources using Partitioned Fixed Priority Scheduling (P-FPS).
The Multiprocessor SRP (MSRP) was proposed by Gai et al. [2], [3] as a P-EDF (Partitioned EDF)-based synchronization protocol for multiprocessors, extending SRP to multiprocessor systems.

Another protocol for multiprocessors is the Flexible Multiprocessor Locking Protocol (FMLP), proposed by Block et al. [4], which is applicable to both partitioned and global scheduling algorithms, i.e., P-EDF and G-EDF. Easwaran and Andersson proposed a synchronization protocol [15] under the global fixed-priority scheduling policy. A schedulability analysis of the Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) under global scheduling algorithms was also presented.

Nemati et al. [16] proposed a locking protocol for resource sharing in independently developed multiprocessor applications. In this work, an interface that abstracts application resource requirements was extended to include resource-sharing aspects.

The main drawback of the lock-based approach is the long blocking times imposed on real-time tasks while waiting for mutually exclusive resources to be released by other tasks. This problem becomes even worse in multicore/multiprocessor systems. The timing analysis for most synchronization protocols proposed for multiprocessor/multicore systems is quite complex and overly pessimistic, accounting for worst-case scenarios that might never occur. Brandenburg [17] proposed using linear programming to reduce pessimism in computing blocking times due to global resource sharing, which improves analysis accuracy at the cost of increased computational complexity.

Wait-free synchronization protocols have been proposed, which are based on providing multiple buffers to prevent tasks from being blocked while waiting for shared resources. Simpson [18] considered the case of multiple readers and writers accessing shared resources and showed that the number of buffers required is 2×n w ×(n r +1), where n w is the number of writers and n r is the number of readers.

Chen and Burns [19] proposed an algorithm to reduce the number of buffers to n r +2 for systems with a single writer and multiple readers. The proposed approach is based on using a consensus protocol between the writer and readers to avoid data corruption during read operations. The approach also avoids the scenario of reading from a buffer that another task is currently writing to.

Tsigas and Zhang [20] presented an algorithm that reduces the number of buffers to n w + n r + 1 for the case of multiple readers and writers. However, the algorithm is limited to cases where the writer task has the highest priority on its processor and includes retry loops.

Other approaches to bounding the number of buffers were proposed by Chen and Burns [6] and Cho et al. [21], using the timing properties of tasks and assuming a single writer and multiple readers. The approach in [6] was later generalized to include multiple writers in [22].

The main drawbacks of the wait-free approach are increased memory requirements and weaker data consistency compared to the lock-based approach, since read operations might access outdated data if the current write has not yet completed.

Combining lock-based and wait-free approaches has shown promising results for improving performance. Baruah proposed a combined approach using multiple buffers and lockbased synchronization [23] to limit blocking times in singleprocessor systems, effectively using multiple replicas of the shared resource.

Di Natale et al. [24] applied a similar principle, formulating an optimization problem to reduce both time delay and memory usage for tasks in single-processor systems. However, both contributions are limited to single-processor systems.

Brandenburg and Anderson [25] generalized the concept of multiple replicas to multicore systems through k-exclusion locks. Nemitz et al. [26] presented three strategies for replica allocation. However, the resources considered in these later works are limited to hardware resources that can be replicated without requiring synchronization.

Finally, an adaptive mechanism was proposed by Usui et al. [27] that combines lock-based and lock-free approaches. At runtime, the mechanism decides whether to use the lock-free or lock-based approach to improve system efficiency; however, this work does not provide any real-time guarantees.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we assume that the multiprocessor (multi-core) platform is composed of m identical cores, CoR 1 , ..., CoR m , which are unit-capacity processors with shared memory executing a number of real-time software applications. Each application consists of n deadline-constrained sporadic hard real-time tasks, denoted as τ i (T i , C i , {Cs i,k,j }, J i , D i ) where T i is a minimum separation time between the arrivals of successive jobs of τ i , C i is their worst-case execution time, J i is the release jitter which is the maximum delay variation in the release time of the task and D i is the relative deadline, satisfying (0 < C i ≤ D i ≤ T i ). Cs i,k,j is the critical section execution time of the kth request issued by τ i that represents the worst-case execution time requirement within a critical section for accessing shared resource R j . Tasks are scheduled using the fixed priority partitioned multiprocessor scheduling approach, where tasks are statically allocated to processors and tasks do not migrate during runtime. Within each core, we assume that each task τ i have unique priority p i . Let {τ } ℓ denote the set of tasks assigned to core CoR ℓ .

Tasks may share resources with other tasks on the same processor or different processors. A shared resource is referred to as a local resource if it is accessed only by tasks on the same processor, and as a global resource if it is accessed by tasks on multiple processors. This paper focuses primarily on global resources, as they often lead to longer blocking times.

We assume that certain global resources can be replicated , provided that the tasks accessing them do not require strong data consistency. For a global resource R j , r replicas are provided, denoted as {R 1 j , ...R r j }. One replica is assigned to each core that has tasks accessing R j . Let τ ℓ j denote the set of tasks on CoRℓ that access R j , i.e., ∀τ i ∈ τ ℓ j , Csi, 1, j > 0. As a result, the number of replicas of R j equals the number of cores with at least one task accessing R j (see Fig. 1).

When a task is granted access to a replica, it may perform a read, write, or read-write operation. We assume that tasks pass an additional parameter with each access request to indicate whether a write operation will be performed. This is important for determining whether the data in the replica will be modified.

We assume that tasks may read older versions of data from replicas, even if newer data has been written to another replica. However, there is an upper bound on how long such stale data remains useful. Let Data Useful Time DU T j i denote the maximum time that old data in replica R ℓ j remains useful for task τ i ∈ τ ℓ j after new data has been written to any replica of R j . For simplicity, we assume that DU T j i is the same for all tasks accessing any replica of R j , and we refer to this as DU T j . If the data useful time varies among tasks, we conservatively define DU T j = min ∀i(DU T j i ). Finally, for simplicity of presentation, we assume that only one global resource is replicated in this paper. MTC utilizes multiple replicas to manage global shared resources effectively. To minimize interference between tasks executed on different cores, each core is assigned its own resource replica of the shared resource. Following the principles of the eventual consistency model used in distributed databases, the data provided by these replicas may not always reflect the most up-to-date values. Nevertheless, the freshness of the data is periodically updated to ensure adequate level of consistency.

div.head: A. MTC protocol
div.p: The MTC protocol works as follows: a) Resource replica access: One replica of a globally shared resource is dedicated to each core, and only tasks within that core can access the replica. The replica can be considered a local resource since no tasks from other cores can access it. Therefore, local synchronization protocols such as SRP can be used to manage access to the resource replica. b) Synchronization tasks: Resource replicas are updated periodically every T U pd . The replica with the latest value is identified and used to update all other replicas. Two additional tasks are introduced in each core that hosts a replica of a global shared resource: τ RLD and τ U DR . The task τ RLD is executed on CoR u , the core whose replica holds the latest data. It copies the data from the replica to a temporary buffer so that other tasks can access it without locking the original replica. The task τ k U DR

updates the replica on CoR k by copying data from the temporary buffer to its local replica. c) Latest data: At every T U pd , MTC identifies the replica R u j with the latest data. Then, τ u RLD is triggered on CoR u . This task accesses the replica using the local synchronization protocol (SRP in this paper). Once access is granted, τ u RLD copies the data to a temporary buffer R temp U DR is triggered on CoR k , it attempts to lock the local replica R k j using the SRP protocol, just like other tasks on that core. Once access is granted, τ k U DR copies the data from R temp j to R k j , but only if the local replica does not already contain newer data. This ensures that updates from local tasks are not overwritten by older data. After updating, τ k U DR releases the replica. Note that at every update period T U pd , the temporary buffer R temp j is updated by τ u RLD , which acts as the writing task. When τ u RLD finishes its execution, it triggers a set of reading tasks τ k U DR on different cores. Multiple simultaneous read operations on R temp j can be performed without synchronization between the reading tasks τ k U DR located on different cores. In addition, there is also no need to synchronize access to R temp j between the writing task τ u RLD and the reading tasks τ k U DR , provided that all reading tasks complete their execution before the next release of τ u RLD . In other words, this is guaranteed if the worst-case response time of each τ k U DR is less than or equal to T U pd .

div.head: B. MTC implementation
div.p: As explained above, at every update period T U pd , the MTC protocol is triggered to determine which replica R u j contains the latest data. Different methods can be used to identify the most recent replica.

div.head: Fig. 2. Circular buffer for tracking latest replica
div.p: • Circular buffer: One method involves using a circular buffer with a size equal to the number of cores that have tasks accessing the global resource, plus one. A pointer (the head of the buffer) always indicates the replica that holds the latest value, as shown in Figure 2. When a task updates the data in a replica, the head of the buffer is advanced by one position, and the identifier of the updated replica or its associated core is stored in the corresponding cell. This mechanism avoids the need for synchronization (i.e., blocking) when multiple update requests arrive simultaneously. This technique typically used in lock-free resource sharing. • Timestamps: Another method is to associate a timestamp with each replica update. Every time a task modifies a replica, it records the time of the update. The replica with the most recent timestamp is then considered to hold the latest data.

Each of these methods has its own advantages and disadvantages. The circular buffer approach requires additional memory and atomic operations to handle simultaneous updates, but it introduces lower runtime overhead. In contrast, the timestamp-based method may incur higher runtime overhead due to the need to read the current time, store it with each update, and compare timestamps across replicas. Since the runtime overhead is platform-dependent, the investigation of the best choice of method is left as future work.

As described in Step 4 in the previous subsection, τ k U DR updates the replica R k j only if its data is older than the data in R temp j . Therefore, it is important for τ k U DR to verify whether R k j has been modified after the MTC protocol identified the latest replica. This verification must cover the interval (v×T U pd +ϵ, t(v, τ k U DR )), where ϵ is the time required to determine the latest replica, and t(v, τ k U DR ) is the time when the v th instance of τ k U DR begins execution.
If the timestamp-based method is used, the timestamp can also be used to determine whether the local replica contains newer data than the temporary buffer.

For the circular buffer method, an additional mechanism is needed to detect updates that occur after the latest replica has been selected. One simple solution is to associate a flag with each replica, which can take one of two values: "changed" or "unchanged." This flag is set to "changed" whenever the replica is modified during the interval (v × T U pd + ϵ, t(v, τ k U DR )). The MTC protocol ensures that the flag can only be modified during this interval. When τ k U DR begins execution at t(v, τ k U DR ), it checks the flag. If the flag indicates that the replica has been changed, the task resets the flag to "unchanged," disables further changes to the flag until the next period, and skips the update to avoid overwriting newer data. To simplify the implementation of MTC, the tasks τ u RLD and τ u U DR on core CoR u can be modeled as a single task, τ u U pd , with two execution modes: RLD and UDR. This task is released every T U pd and operates as follows: a) If R u j is identified as the latest replica, τ u U pd runs in RLD mode. b) If another core CoR p executes τ p U pd in RLD mode and determines that CoR u must update its replica, it triggers τ u U pd to run in UDR mode. As a result, at each update period T U pd , τ u U pd executes in only one mode on core CoR u . Figure 3 shows an execution trace example of the proposed solution. An important observation regarding the scheduling of τ u U pd is that it may experience release jitter. Consider the release time of τ 1 U pd on CoR 1 . In the first instance (between t 1 and t 3 ), it is released at t 2 , which includes both the execution time of τ 3 U pd and the blocking time experienced on CoR 3 after the start of the update period at t 1 . In the second instance (after t 3 ), τ 1 U pd is released immediately after τ 2 U pd completes, assuming τ 2 U pd was not blocked. Even if τ 2 U pd and τ 3 U pd have the same execution time, the release time of τ 1 U pd may still vary. This variability can be modeled as release jitter and may impact the schedulability of tasks on the cores. The evaluation of this jitter will be presented in the next section. Finally, the time required to determine which replica holds the latest data is modeled as an overhead. This overhead can be added to the execution time of τ u U pd and is assumed to be relatively small.

div.head: C. Timing analysis
div.p: The design and implementation of the MTC protocol are specifically aimed at decoupling, as much as possible, the timing analysis of tasks on one core from those on other cores. Since each replica serves only the tasks on its assigned core, there is no direct dependency between tasks located on different coreseven if they share the same global resource. The only direct interaction arises from the updating tasks, which execute periodically and are synchronized as described in previous sections. A temporary buffer is used to eliminate potential interference between updating tasks and local tasks. The only remaining dependency that cannot be fully removed is the interaction among updating tasks due to release jitter, as previously explained. Since the SRP protocol 2 is used by all tasksincluding τ u U pd in both RLD and UDR modesto manage access to local resources, the existing timing analysis for SRP can be applied. In SRP, each shared resource is assigned a ceiling priority equal to the highest priority of the tasks that access it. In general, the worst-case response time of a task τ u scheduled under fixed-priority scheduling and using SRP on core CoR u can be evaluated using the traditional worst-case response time analysis, as shown below.

div.head: D. MTC protocol properties
div.p: In this section, we demonstrate the properties of MTC protocol by identifying which parameters might affect the worst-case response times (WCRT) of tasks. In addition, we compare it with a lock-based protocol called FLMP-Short [28]. We use a qualitative evaluation method intentionally avoiding extensive simulations. The protocol analysis is a straightforward extension of the well-known worst-case response time analysis in the real-time systems community. Similarly, we chose the lock-based protocol FMLP-Short due to its ease of integration with worst-case response time analysis. The parameters that impact performance can be easily estimated from the equations provided in the analysis. We show that a fair comparison between MTC and most lock based protocols is not possible due to the differing influential parameters. In FMLP-Short [28], whenever a task on one core tries to access a shared global resource that is already locked by a task on another core, it busy-waits non-preemptively until the resource becomes available. A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue is used to manage multiple busywaiting tasks across different cores. When a task locks a global resource, it executes non-preemptively until it releases the resource, after which it resumes execution at its normal priority. The traditional worst-case response time analysis for local resource sharing can be extended to FMLP-Short by boosting the execution times of all tasks that access global shared resources. This is done by adding the maximum blocking time from each core that has tasks sharing the same resource. Additionally, the resource ceiling is set to the highest-priority task in each core to prevent preemption during busy-waiting and resource access. Finally, the blocking time from lower-priority tasks should be boosted in a similar way as the tasks execution times. Looking at Eq 2, since the implementation of managing shared resource is modeled as a normal task τ k U pd the parameters of τ k U pd have the main impact on the WCRT of tasks in each core. The period T k U pd , C k U pd , J k U pd , and the priority of τ k U pd will affect the performance in terms of shorter or longer WCRT for tasks. Increasing T k U pd will have positive impact as it will derease the number of instances that the tasks interfere with the lower priority tasks, this parameter has direct impact on the quality of control for control applications, the lower the value is the best it will be. C k U pd depends on the size of the data while J k U pd depends on the blocking times and the priority of τ k U pd in other cores as shown in Eq 3. Finally, the priority of τ k U pd has also significant impact on WCRT of tasks in the core as the lower the priority is the less tasks being preempted by τ k U pd . Inceasing number of cores that have tasks access global shared resources has no impact on MTC, while increasing the size of critical sections while having indirect impact on the jitter J k U pd . For FMLP-short, it does not use a task to manage the updates of shared resources, however, since the execution times and blocking times are boosted as explained above then increasing number of core and increasing the size of blocking time (critical section execution time) will have big impact on WCRT of all tasks. Increasing the number of tasks that access the global share resource in each core or even increasing the number of time a task access the same resource have also big impact as the execution times and blocking times of these tasks should be boosted and will have direct effect on the WCRT for FMLP-short, while for MTC it will not have similar impact as these might add local blocking time in each core. For MTC, the impact of the updating tasks period (T U pd ) and execution time (C U pd ) is shown. For FLMP-Short, we consider 2-and 4-core setups, where remote blocking equals the longest critical section on other cores. In summary, depending on the setting and requirements, MTC might even provide better results than the locked based protocols, however, this might not be always the case and since the parameters that affect the performance are different then individual evaluation should be applied. However, in addition to simplified timing analysis MTC can provide other advantages that lock based protocols can not. Due to the use of multiple replicas, MTC can provide isolation among tasks executed in different cores, which is extremely important in case if a fault occurs in one of the replicas. For example, if a task locks a resource without releasing it, tasks in other cores will not be affected, and a rollback can easily be implemented since a copy of the data exists in other replicas. MTC provides fault tolerance for real-time tasks. In addition, in case of sharing resources among safety-critical applications and no safety-critical application located in different cores than the safety-critical applications, the protocol might be adapted such that it updates the data only from trusted replicas associated with the cores that have safety-critical applications. Finally, since replicas can be considered as local shared resources in each core, nested access to global shared resources will not be an a problem as it is in most lock-based solutions proposed for multicore systems. In this paper, we proposed a new synchronization protocol, MTC, for real-time tasks executing on a multiprocessor platform. The protocol combines lock-based and wait-free synchronization to protect shared resources.

The goal of MTC is to reduce the response time of realtime tasks by minimizing the blocking time imposed by purely lock-based solutions, while also reducing the memory requirements associated with purely waitfree approaches. The protocol is applicable to real-time systems with limited memory and timing resources, where neither exclusive lock-based nor wait-free synchronization is feasible.

In addition, the proposed approach may be suitable for more general real-time systems, as it allows for performance optimizationfor example, by reducing task response times while using less memory. MTC isolates the impact of global resource usage among tasks located on different cores, enabling the use of relatively simple and well-known response time analysis techniques that support local resource sharing. Our ongoing work focuses on further reducing the impact of global resource sharing. One research direction is to extend the protocol to support multiple globally shared resources. This would require each core to run multiple updating tasks that synchronize replicas of these resources. Assigning priorities to these tasks presents an interesting optimization problem, as it can significantly influence the response times of other tasks. Another direction involves developing resource-sharingaware algorithms for task-to-core allocation, taking the MTC protocol into account. Such algorithms could help minimize interference and improve overall system performance by strategically placing tasks based on their resource access patterns and timing requirements.
